nameStory: The "rough" in rough cinquefoil comes from the coarse, hairy texture of its stems and leaves that feel scratchy to the touch. Despite being called "Norwegian cinquefoil," this hardy wildflower isn't exclusively from Norway—it's actually native across much of northern Europe, Asia, and parts of North America.
description: Rough cinquefoil is a weedy annual wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with a branching, upright habit. It produces small yellow flowers with five petals throughout the growing season, typical of the rose family. The plant has a distinctly rough, hairy texture and three-part leaves that distinguish it from many of its cinquefoil cousins. You'll often find it growing in disturbed soils, gardens, and waste areas where its opportunistic nature helps it thrive.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-leaflet compound leaves (like a clover) with toothed edges, arranged alternately on the stem. Each leaflet is oval-shaped and feels rough and hairy to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flowers about 1/4 inch across with five rounded petals. Flowers appear singly or in small clusters at the tips of branches and have a simple, open-faced appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, branching annual that grows 1-3 feet tall with multiple stems from the base. The whole plant has a somewhat scraggly, weedy appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly hairy and rough-textured stems that feel coarse when you run your fingers along them. The hairs are stiff and give the plant its "rough" common name.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny dry seeds clustered together in a small, rounded head that replaces each flower. The seed head is much less conspicuous than the yellow blooms.

habitat: Rough cinquefoil thrives in disturbed soils, roadsides, gardens, vacant lots, and waste areas throughout New England. It prefers full sun to partial shade and adapts well to poor, compacted soils where other plants struggle. You'll commonly spot it growing alongside other weedy species in agricultural areas and urban environments.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and develop their characteristic three-part leaves. Early flowering may begin in late spring in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with small yellow flowers appearing continuously. Plants reach full size and are most easily identified during this season.
seasonality.fall: Continued flowering into early fall, with seed production ramping up. Plants begin to look more weathered and may turn brown after first frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil. No above-ground parts remain visible.

funFact: Despite its name suggesting Norwegian origins, rough cinquefoil is such a successful traveler that botanists aren't entirely sure where it originally came from—it may have been hopping between continents and spreading naturally long before humans started moving plants around!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other cinquefoils, but rough cinquefoil's three-part leaves make it distinctive—most other cinquefoils have five leaflets (hence "cinquefoil" meaning "five leaves"). Remember: "Rough has three, others have five."
contextualKnowledge: The name "cinquefoil" comes from French meaning "five leaves," but rough cinquefoil breaks this rule with its three leaflets, making it something of an oddball in the genus. This can confuse beginners who expect all cinquefoils to follow the five-leaflet pattern.
compareHints: Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf. It's also annual rather than perennial like many of its relatives, and tends to be much more upright and branched compared to the often low-growing or creeping habits of species like dwarf cinquefoil or common cinquefoil.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
